title: Feminist Theory
summary: How feminists read world politics through gender, why that matters for IR, and the radical, liberal, Marxist and critical strands.

sections.name: Gender as a lens on IR

lesson.title: Sex, gender and a gendered world
lesson.hook: Look at a photo of any ECOWAS summit. Count the women. Feminists say that empty space is not an accident; it tells you something about how world politics is built.

slides.heading: A theory that looks through gender
slides.body:
**Feminist theory** views international relations mainly from a **gender perspective**. It asks how world politics affects men and women, and how men and women in turn shape world politics.

It also makes a sharper claim: the core concepts of the discipline, such as **war, security and power**, are themselves **gendered**. They were built around men's experiences and male-coded values, and then presented as neutral.

left.title: Sex
points: Biological difference
Male and female bodies
Largely given at birth

right.title: Gender
points: Socially constructed identities
Masculine and feminine roles
Relationship between the sexes
Varies across societies

slides.heading: Four things to get right first
slides.body: First, feminism studies **gender**, not just women, and the difference gender makes to world politics. Second, it examines how **masculine and feminine** are linked, socially built categories that shape how we see the world. Third, because roles are **socially constructed**, feminists question any fixed idea of what women 'naturally' are. Fourth, you do not have to be a woman to be a feminist: anyone, **male or female**, concerned with gender issues can be one.

slides.question: In feminist theory, 'gender' refers mainly to:
options: The biological difference between male and female
The social construction of men's and women's identities in relation to each other
The number of women in parliament
slides.why: Gender is about socially built identities and the relationship between the sexes. Biological difference is 'sex', which feminists insist is not the same thing.

slides.heading: Roots in a movement
slides.body:
Modern feminism grew out of the **women's liberation movement**, a protest against gender-based power structures and the accepted norms about men and women.

The protest took different forms. Some demanded that women be allowed into spheres historically reserved for men, such as parliament, the army or the boardroom. Others demanded deeper, more **fundamental social change**. This split foreshadows the strands of feminism you will meet later.

slides.heading: Power between men and women
slides.body:
Feminists analyse **relations of power between men and women**: how that power is exercised and how it has been built up through habit, history and society over time. Crucially, they deny it comes from **inherent biological differences**.

They argue that in almost every part of the world women remain **second-class citizens** economically, politically and socially, and that society is arranged so men benefit at women's expense.

slides.heading: Who cooks for the summit?
slides.story: At a big conference in Abuja, Tunde reports on the ministers and generals in the hall. Few are women. Outside, women run the food stalls, clean the venue and care for the delegates' children at home. The newspapers call the summit 'international relations'; nobody calls the cooking and childcare that.
slides.takeaway: Feminists ask why the public, male-dominated sphere counts as IR while women's work in the private sphere stays invisible.

slides.heading: Beyond war and diplomacy
slides.body:
Feminist IR studies the traditional topics of **states, wars, diplomacy and security**, but also looks at how gender shapes the **global political economy**: who works in factories, who sends remittances, who does unpaid care.

Its key questions are: Where do 'women' and 'men' fit in IR? How do constructed genders affect world politics? How is the international system, and the study of IR, itself gendered?

slides.question: Feminists argue that the international system has a strongly masculine orientation. Which observation best supports this claim?
options: Women are naturally more peaceful than men
Men hold most prominent positions while women are pushed into a 'domestic sphere'
International law forbids women from holding office
slides.why: Men dominate the visible public roles while women are confined to a largely invisible private sphere. Feminists reject both the 'naturally peaceful' and purely biological claims.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: The classic trap is confusing sex with gender, or saying feminism is 'the study of women' only. Lecturers also set objectives asking who can be a feminist. Use Cynthia Enloe's question 'Where are the women?' to show you have read beyond the manual.
slides.sampleQuestion: 'Feminism in IR is the study of gender, not women.' Discuss.
slides.howToAnswer: Distinguish sex from gender, explain gender as socially constructed and relational, and show that feminists study how masculine and feminine shape core IR concepts like security and power.

points: Feminist theory views IR through a gender lens.
Sex is biological; gender is the social construction of identities in relation to each other.
Feminism studies gender, not only women; men can be feminists.
It grew from the women's liberation movement.
It covers war and security and also the global political economy.

questions.stem: Feminists insist that 'gender' is not a synonym for 'sex' because gender refers to:
options: Biological differences between men and women
Socially constructed identities and behaviours of men and women
questions.explanation: Gender is the social construction of identities in relation to each other. Biological, hormonal and chromosomal traits belong to 'sex'.

questions.stem: Contemporary feminism has its roots in which social movement?
questions.explanation: Modern feminism grew from the women's liberation movement, which protested gender-based power structures. The Non-Aligned Movement was a Cold War grouping of states.

questions.stem: According to feminist theory, who can be a feminist?
options: Anyone, male or female, concerned with gender issues
questions.explanation: Feminists include all who are concerned with gender, whether male or female. Restricting it to women is a common misconception.

questions.stem: Feminists claim that concepts such as war, security and power are 'gendered'. This means that these concepts:
options: Were shaped around male experiences and masculine values yet presented as neutral
questions.explanation: Feminists argue core IR concepts carry masculine assumptions while appearing neutral. Saying they apply only to women gets the point backwards.

questions.stem: Feminists explain the unequal power between men and women mainly as the result of:
options: Habit, history and social practice over time
questions.explanation: Feminists see the power gap as built up historically and socially, not from biology. Anarchy is a realist explanation for state behaviour.

questions.stem: Beyond states, wars and diplomacy, feminist IR has stressed how gender shapes:
questions.explanation: Feminists highlight the gendered nature of the global political economy, such as unpaid care and low-wage factory work. The other options are outside IR.

questions.stem: Amaka argues that because roles like 'caregiver' and 'warrior' are learned, we should not assume we know what women naturally are. Her argument reflects the feminist view that gender roles are:
questions.explanation: Feminists see gender roles as socially constructed, so they question fixed ideas of feminine nature. 'Determined by the economy alone' is closer to a crude Marxist claim.

questions.stem: A researcher counts that most foreign ministers, generals and IR professors are men, while women's work is largely in the home. A feminist would use this to argue that:
options: The international system has a masculine orientation that renders women invisible
The balance of power favours small states
questions.explanation: Feminists see male dominance of prominent roles and women's confinement to the domestic sphere as evidence of a masculine system. They reject biological and 'lack of interest' explanations.

questions.stem: Two activists disagree: one wants women admitted into the army and parliament; the other wants society completely transformed. Both positions are consistent with:
options: The range of demands within the feminist movement
questions.explanation: Feminist protest has ranged from entry into male spheres to fundamental social change. Neither demand is a realist or functionalist position.

questions.stem: Which statement about feminist theory is NOT correct?
options: It studies the interdependence of masculine and feminine
It treats gender as a socially constructed category
It is concerned only with women and ignores men
It examines how IR as a discipline is gendered
questions.explanation: Feminism studies gender, which includes men and masculinity, not women alone. The other statements are accurate.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Gender – relationship between the sexes in a society
questions.explanation: Gender describes the relationship between the sexes in a given society. The other pairs swap the meanings of sex and gender.

questions.stem: The question 'Where are the women?' in international politics is most closely associated with:
questions.explanation: Enloe's Bananas, Beaches and Bases (1989) asked where women are in world politics. Cox is a critical theorist; Morgenthau and Waltz are realists.

questions.stem: Consider: I. Feminism is the study of gender rather than only women. II. Feminists accept that gender inequality is biologically determined. III. Men can be feminists. IV. Feminists ask how IR studies are themselves gendered. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: Feminists reject biological explanations of inequality, so II is false. I, III and IV are correct statements.

questions.stem: A realist claims that 'security' simply means protecting the state from military attack. A feminist critique would most likely reply that:
options: Security is a purely biological matter
This definition is neutral and should not be questioned
This view is gendered, overlooking insecurities such as domestic violence and economic exclusion
Only women can define security correctly
questions.explanation: Feminists argue that core concepts like security are gendered and ignore insecurities women face. They do not claim only women can define security.

questions.stem: Which combination best captures feminism's approach to world politics?
options: Gender as a social construction plus attention to power between men and women
Class struggle plus surplus value only
questions.explanation: Feminism combines a view of gender as constructed with analysis of gendered power relations. Human nature and anarchy are realist foundations.

lesson.title: Making gender visible in world politics
lesson.hook: When the news reports women as Boko Haram suicide bombers, many people are shocked: 'women are supposed to be peaceful'. Feminists say that shock reveals a hidden assumption worth examining.

slides.heading: Late arrival
slides.body:
Feminist IR emerged mainly from the **late 1980s**. Before then, women and gender were **ignored or marginalised** in the discipline.

The **end of the Cold War** and the rethinking of traditional theories in the **1990s** opened space for 'gendering' IR. Once the old superpower contest no longer dominated every debate, scholars could ask questions that had long been pushed aside.

slides.heading: Male players, competitive politics
slides.body:
Feminists note that most key players in IR, such as **policymakers, heads of government and academics**, have been and still are **men from patriarchal backgrounds**.

They argue that IR is **competitive, power-oriented and exploitative** largely because of this male domination. Socially built gender identities shape how power is distributed, and that decides where women stand in global politics.

slides.heading: Expected masculinity and femininity
slides.body:
Men can be feminine and women can be masculine. But societies **expect** masculinity of men and femininity of women, and reward people who conform.

Feminists argue that IR would be **more balanced and effective** if women had their due share of politics. So a key goal is to **increase women's participation** and the positions they hold at all levels, and to improve women's lot in the international system.

slides.question: Feminist IR emerged largely from which period?
options: Immediately after the First World War
slides.why: Feminist IR took shape from the late 1980s, helped by the end of the Cold War. Idealism, not feminism, followed the First World War.

slides.heading: Challenging 'peaceful victim' images
slides.body:
Feminist theory challenges the picture of women as **naturally peaceful**, as **needing protection** or as **victims**. These images are themselves evidence of inequality.

When women are pictured only as victims, never as actors, as gentle by nature, and as belonging at home instead of in public life, what they actually do gets brushed aside as minor. Cases of women as **agents of political violence** break these stereotypes.

slides.heading: The Aba Women's War
slides.story: In 1929, thousands of Igbo and Ibibio women in south-eastern Nigeria rose against colonial warrant chiefs and feared taxation of women. They organised across villages, besieged officials and forced the British to change the system. Colonial reports had treated these women as passive; their action proved them political agents.
slides.takeaway: Treating women only as passive or peaceful hides their real role in politics, which feminists insist on recovering.

slides.question: Why do feminists object to portraying women mainly as peaceful victims needing protection?
options: Because women are biologically more violent
Because such images make it easier to ignore women's experiences and keep them from power
Because victims are not part of IR
slides.why: These images push women's perspectives to the margins and limit their access to power. Feminists do not claim women are biologically more violent.

slides.heading: A fuller picture of world politics
slides.body:
Taking feminism seriously is not only about correcting women's historic exclusion. It gives a **more complete picture** of global politics by counting a wider range of **actors and actions**.

Feminists want the link between **global order and gender relations** made visible, so we understand how humanity as a whole shapes, and is shaped by, the global system. IR, they argue, rests on and repeats gendered ideas about who does what and who suffers what.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: 'Examine the importance of feminist theory to IR' is a standard essay. Weak answers just say 'women are oppressed'. Strong ones cover timing (late 1980s, end of Cold War), male domination of policy, the challenge to 'peaceful victim' images and the fuller picture of world politics. A real example lifts your grade.
slides.sampleQuestion: Why does feminist theory matter for understanding world politics today? Argue your case.
slides.howToAnswer: Explain how feminism exposes male domination and gendered concepts, challenges stereotypes of women as passive, pushes for women's participation, and broadens the actors IR studies. Illustrate with cases such as UN Security Council Resolution 1325 (2000).

points: Feminist IR emerged from the late 1980s; the Cold War's end gave it space.
Key IR players remain mostly men from patriarchal backgrounds.
Feminists link competitive, exploitative IR to male domination.
They seek more women in decision-making at all levels.
They reject images of women as only peaceful victims, giving a fuller picture of IR.

questions.stem: Which development in the 1990s opened space for 'gendering' International Relations?
options: The founding of the League of Nations
The end of the Cold War and re-evaluation of traditional theory
questions.explanation: The end of the Cold War and rethinking of traditional theories in the 1990s made room for gender analysis. The League and Westphalia belong to much earlier periods.

questions.stem: One major goal of feminists in IR is to:
options: Increase women's participation in political decision-making at all levels
questions.explanation: Feminists seek greater participation of women in politics and better positions for them. The other goals are not feminist aims.

questions.stem: Feminists attribute the competitive, power-oriented and exploitative nature of IR mainly to:
questions.explanation: Feminists link the aggressive character of IR to male domination of political life. Democracy and trade are not their explanation.

questions.stem: According to feminists, socially constructed gender identities matter in IR because they:
options: Shape how power is distributed and where women stand in global politics
questions.explanation: Gender identities determine distributions of power that place women in global politics. Feminists reject the idea that they are fixed by biology.

questions.stem: Feminists argue that taking gender seriously in IR provides:
options: A narrower focus on military power
A more complete picture of global politics with more actors and actions
Proof that states are unitary actors
A replacement for all economic analysis
questions.explanation: Feminism broadens the range of actors and actions studied, giving a fuller account. It does not narrow analysis to military power.

questions.stem: Before the late 1980s, women and gender issues in the study of IR were mostly:
questions.explanation: Gender was largely ignored or pushed to the margins before feminist IR emerged. Realism, idealism and structuralism did not centre it.

questions.stem: News reports express surprise that women carried out attacks for an armed group. A feminist analyst would most likely say this surprise reflects:
options: A gendered assumption that women are naturally peaceful
Proof that women are biologically violent
The absence of gender in politics
questions.explanation: Feminists see the 'peaceful women' image as a gendered construction that cases of female political violence disrupt. They do not argue for biological violence.

questions.stem: Women in 1929 south-eastern Nigeria organised against colonial taxation and forced policy changes. Feminists would use this case mainly to show that:
options: Women only act in the domestic sphere
Women have been political actors despite being portrayed as passive
Gender has no bearing on resistance
questions.explanation: The Aba Women's War shows women acting in the public political sphere, challenging images of women as passive. It contradicts the idea that women only act at home.

questions.stem: Ngozi became the first woman to head a major global trade body. A feminist would see her appointment mainly as:
options: Proof that gender inequality has ended worldwide
A step toward increasing women's share of international decision-making
questions.explanation: Feminists seek more women in decision-making positions, so such appointments are progress. One appointment does not mean inequality has ended.

questions.stem: Feminists argue that images of women as victims, in need of protection, or confined to the private realm are harmful mainly because they:
options: Make women's perspectives easier to dismiss and limit their access to power
Are accurate descriptions of all women
questions.explanation: Such constructions marginalise women's experiences and help keep them out of power. Feminists do not see them as accurate for all women.

questions.stem: Which statement about masculinity and femininity is consistent with feminist theory?
options: Masculinity is biologically fixed in men
Men can be feminine and women masculine, but society expects the reverse
questions.explanation: Feminists accept that both sexes can show either trait, but social expectations tie masculinity to men and femininity to women. That expectation has political effects.

questions.stem: Who wrote 'Gendering World Politics' (2001), a key text of feminist IR?
questions.explanation: J. Ann Tickner wrote Gendering World Politics. Wallerstein is a world-systems theorist and Linklater a critical theorist.

questions.stem: Consider: I. Feminist IR emerged mainly in the late 1980s. II. Feminists say most IR policymakers come from patriarchal backgrounds. III. Feminists accept the image of women as inherently peaceful. IV. Feminists want the link between global order and gender relations made visible. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: Feminists challenge the image of women as inherently peaceful, so III is false. The other three statements are correct.

questions.stem: A student says, 'Feminism in IR is just about adding a few women to the list of leaders.' The strongest feminist rebuttal is that feminism also:
options: Denies that men have any role in IR
Shows how IR concepts and practices rest on gendered assumptions and widens what counts as IR
Rejects the study of states entirely
questions.explanation: Feminism goes beyond adding women; it exposes gendered assumptions and broadens the actors and actions IR studies. It does not reject states or men.

questions.stem: A researcher concludes that a war ministry's policies reflect gendered ideas about who fights and who is protected. Which feminist claim does this best support?
options: IR rests on, and repeats, gendered ideas about who does what in global politics
War is caused by international anarchy alone
questions.explanation: The finding supports the feminist claim that IR depends on gendered ideas about roles. Anarchy alone is a realist explanation.

lesson.title: Radical, liberal, Marxist and critical feminism
lesson.hook: Four feminists walk into a seminar. They all want gender equality, yet they disagree about the enemy: men, discrimination, capitalism, or ideas. Knowing which is which is a sure exam question.

slides.heading: One goal, several roads
slides.body:
Like most IR theories, feminism has **several strands**. All share the agenda of **gender equality**, but they differ in their assumptions about the cause of women's oppression and the cure.

This course covers four: **radical**, **liberal**, **Marxist** and **critical** feminism. A useful trick is to ask of each: what is the root problem, and what is the solution?

slides.heading: Radical feminism
slides.body:
**Radical feminism** argues that oppression of women came **first**, reaches **furthest**, and cuts **deepest** of all forms of oppression. The basic division in every society is between **men and women**, with men as oppressors.

Radical feminists developed the concept of **patriarchy** to explain institutionalised male domination, showing gender is not just a matter of personal identity. Oppression of women as women is more basic than class, ethnic or religious oppression. The aim: **overthrow patriarchy** and radically reorder society.

slides.heading: Liberal feminism
slides.body:
**Liberal feminism** says **participation in public life** is the key to improving women's status. It asks for **no special privileges**, only equal consideration without sex discrimination.

Women, like men, are **rational and equally intelligent**, so they belong in public life, not only the home. Perceived differences are effects of **discrimination**. Change can come **without restructuring society**, through education, political mobilisation, better laws and removing institutional bias, with the **state** as a helper.

slides.question: Which strand believes women's status can improve without changing the basic structure of society?
slides.why: Liberal feminists rely on equal rights, education and better laws within the existing order. Radical and Marxist feminists call for deep structural change.

slides.heading: Marxist feminism
slides.body:
**Marxist feminism** sees **dismantling capitalism** as the route to women's liberation. **Private property** is the root of oppression, producing economic inequality and dependence.

Gender oppression is a form of **class oppression**: man is to woman as **bourgeoisie** is to **proletariat**. Capitalism split the **public realm of work** from the **private realm of home**, reducing women and children to men's property and hiding the value of women's **unpaid domestic labour** to the economy.

slides.heading: Mama Bisi's unpaid shift
slides.story: Mama Bisi wakes at five to fetch water, cook, get the children ready and care for her sick mother-in-law before opening her shop. Her husband's factory wage is counted in the national accounts; her hours of housework are not. Without her, he could not work at all.
slides.takeaway: Marxist feminists say capitalism depends on women's unpaid domestic labour while treating it as worthless.

slides.heading: Critical feminism
slides.body:
**Critical feminism** borrows from Marxism but stresses how **ideas about gender legitimise inequality**. A socially relevant difference is used to justify treating men and women differently, so gender becomes **institutionalised** in practice.

It sees the **state as patriarchal** where it backs institutions like **marriage** that sustain male dominance, defining women as **dependants**, wives and mothers, which limits their citizenship. Yet the state is also a site where patriarchy is both **constructed and contested**.

slides.question: Which strand views the state as a set of power relations in which patriarchy is both constructed and contested?
slides.why: Critical feminists see the state as patriarchal yet open to contest. Liberal feminists see the state more simply as a tool for better laws.

left.title: Radical and Marxist
points: Radical: patriarchy is the root
Radical: overthrow it, reorder society
Marxist: private property and capitalism
Marxist: dismantle capitalism

right.title: Liberal and critical
points: Liberal: discrimination and barriers
Liberal: equal rights, laws, education
Critical: gender ideas legitimise inequality
Critical: expand women's autonomy

terms.meaning: Gender is the central unit of analysis, viewed through 'gender lenses'.
Gender is a particular kind of power relationship.
The split between spheres is central to understanding IR.
Gender ideas shape how international institutions work; their laws can sustain or change gender relations.
Gender is built into world order; feminists challenge what counts as central or marginal.
More women in national and international decisions and economic life.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'which strand is matched with which claim' objectives and 'analyse four strands' essays. The big trap: mixing up radical (patriarchy, men as oppressors) with Marxist (capitalism, private property), or calling liberal feminists revolutionaries. Remember that liberals want equality without special privileges.
slides.sampleQuestion: Analyse any four strands of feminist theory, showing how each explains the oppression of women.
slides.howToAnswer: For each strand give the root cause and remedy: radical (patriarchy; overthrow it), liberal (discrimination; equal rights within existing society), Marxist (capitalism and private property; end capitalism), critical (gender ideas legitimising inequality; expand autonomy, contest the patriarchal state).

points: All strands seek gender equality but differ on cause and cure.
Radical: patriarchy is the deepest oppression; reorder society.
Liberal: equal participation through laws and education, no special privileges.
Marxist: capitalism and private property oppress women; unpaid labour is hidden.
Critical: gender ideas legitimise inequality; the state is patriarchal but contested.
Feminists use gender as a central category and a form of power.

questions.stem: Which strand of feminism developed the concept of patriarchy to explain institutionalised male domination?
questions.explanation: Radical feminists developed patriarchy to show male domination is institutionalised. Marxist feminists locate the root in capitalism instead.

questions.stem: Marxist feminists see the root of women's oppression in:
options: Private property and the capitalist mode of production
questions.explanation: Marxist feminists blame private property and capitalism for women's subordination. Lack of education is closer to a liberal feminist concern.

questions.stem: Liberal feminists believe the key to advancing women's status is:
options: Participation in public life on equal terms
questions.explanation: Liberal feminists see equal participation in public life as the key. Overthrowing patriarchy is the radical feminist goal.

questions.stem: Radical feminists hold that oppression of women is:
options: The first, most widespread and deepest form of oppression
Caused mainly by the state system
questions.explanation: Radical feminists see women's oppression as more fundamental than class, ethnic or religious oppression. Seeing it as an effect of discrimination is the liberal view.

questions.stem: Which statement about liberal feminism is NOT correct?
options: It seeks equal consideration without sex discrimination
It demands special privileges for women above men
It sees women as rational and equally intelligent
It believes better laws can improve women's status
questions.explanation: Liberal feminists explicitly seek no special privileges, only equal treatment. The other statements accurately describe the strand.

questions.stem: Critical feminists stress the importance of ideas about gender because such ideas:
options: Legitimise social inequality between men and women
questions.explanation: Critical feminists argue gender ideas justify differential treatment and become institutionalised. They reject the view that gender is biologically fixed.

questions.stem: An activist argues that the real enemy of women is capitalism, which separated paid work from the home and made women's housework invisible. This activist is a:
questions.explanation: Linking women's oppression to capitalism and the public–private split of work is Marxist feminism. Radical feminists would blame patriarchy, not capitalism.

questions.stem: Kemi campaigns for scholarships for girls, equal pay laws and an end to sex discrimination in hiring, but does not seek to overturn the social system. Her position is closest to:
questions.explanation: Equal rights through education and laws within the existing order is liberal feminism. Radical and Marxist feminists demand structural change.

questions.stem: A scholar argues that the state upholds marriage laws that define women as dependants, limiting their citizenship, but that women can also contest these laws through the state. This is the view of:
questions.explanation: Critical feminists see the state as patriarchal through institutions like marriage, yet as a site where patriarchy is contested. Liberal feminists see the state mainly as a reform tool.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Radical feminism – women's subordination as class oppression
Marxist feminism – men as the primary oppressors of women
Liberal feminism – perceived gender differences as effects of discrimination
Critical feminism – change without any role for ideas
questions.explanation: Liberal feminists treat perceived differences as products of discrimination. Class oppression belongs to Marxist feminism and 'men as oppressors' to radical feminism.

questions.stem: In Marxist feminism, the relationship between men and women is compared to the relationship between:
questions.explanation: Marxist feminists see the man–woman relationship as similar to that between bourgeoisie and proletariat. Core and periphery is structuralist vocabulary for states.

questions.stem: All of the following are basic assumptions of feminist theory EXCEPT:
options: Gender is a central category of analysis
Gender is a particular kind of power relationship
The division between public and private spheres is central to IR
Gender is irrelevant to international institutions
questions.explanation: Feminists trace how gender ideas shape international institutions and their policies. The first three options are listed feminist assumptions.

questions.stem: Consider: I. Radical feminism seeks to overthrow patriarchy. II. Liberal feminism requires restructuring society before change can occur. III. Marxist feminism sees capitalism as the root of women's oppression. IV. Critical feminism sees the state as a site where patriarchy is constructed and contested. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: Liberal feminists believe change can happen without altering the structure of society, so II is false. I, III and IV are correct.

questions.stem: A radical feminist and a Marxist feminist both condemn women's oppression. The key difference between them is that:
options: The radical feminist sees gender oppression as more basic than class; the Marxist feminist treats it as a form of class oppression
Both see private property as the root cause
The Marxist feminist rejects any link between gender and economics
The radical feminist seeks equality through gradual legal reform
questions.explanation: Radical feminists place gender oppression above class, while Marxist feminists fold it into class oppression under capitalism. Gradual legal reform is the liberal approach.

questions.stem: A UN agency changes its loan rules after finding they excluded women farmers. Which pair of feminist assumptions does this case best illustrate?
options: Gender is biological; institutions are neutral
Gender shapes how international institutions work; their policies can perpetuate or change gender relations
Gender is irrelevant to the economy; women belong in the private sphere
Anarchy drives policy; gender is marginal
questions.explanation: The case shows gender built into an institution's rules and changed through policy. Wait: the correct choice is the second option, which states exactly this; the third contradicts feminist assumptions.
